title: The Universe Is Too Big for Video Games — Here’s How Devs Fake It
summary:
Space is incomprehensibly vast. The observable universe spans 93 billion light-years; our Milky Way alone is 100,000 light-years across. At Artemis 2 speeds (25,000 mph), reaching Alpha Centauri would take 80,000 years. For game developers, this poses a fundamental design conflict: how to convey the awe of cosmic scale without subjecting players to eons of empty, boring travel.

Astrophysicist Dr. Jeffrey Bennett illustrates the problem: on a 1-to-10-billion scale, the Sun is a grapefruit, Earth a pinhead 49 feet away, and the Moon just 1.5 inches distant. Walking to the outermost planets takes 10 minutes, but reaching the nearest star means trekking across the entire United States. Most sci-fi games and films get this wrong, making interstellar travel look easy and asteroid fields dangerously dense. In reality, asteroids are typically hundreds of thousands of kilometers apart — accidental collisions are virtually impossible.

Bernd Lehahn, founder of Egosoft (X4: Foundations), acknowledges the tension: “Space must feel very large, or else players will feel cheated. At the same time, most games do not want to force players through unnecessarily long flight times or, god forbid, boredom.” His team balances dense, fast-travel hubs with remote, empty frontiers to evoke both bustle and isolation.

Technical tricks help: level-of-detail scaling, instancing, and streaming create the illusion of vastness without melting hardware. Yet the core challenge remains: compressing space too much feels artificial, but realism means interminable black voids. The solution is an artful compromise, one that continues to evolve with each new game.
why_it_matters: As games become more immersive, understanding how developers fake space can inspire interest in real astronomy. The tricks that compress the universe may also be used in virtual-reality education tools, making it easier to explore and appreciate the true dimensions of our cosmos.

background_read: The true scale of space is almost impossible for the human mind to grasp. Even our solar system’s outermost planets are so distant that light from the Sun takes hours to reach them, and the nearest star, Alpha Centauri (just 4.37 light-years away), is still 25 trillion miles from Earth. NASA’s Artemis 2 mission, intended to carry astronauts around the Moon, would crawl at 25,000 mph compared to interstellar distances.

Game developers have grappled with this since early space sims. Dr. Jeffrey Bennett, an astrophysicist and science educator, created a famous scale model where the Sun is a grapefruit and Earth a pinhead 49 feet away; walking to the nearest star would cross the entire United States. Such comparisons highlight why games compress space.

The German studio Egosoft, founded by Bernd Lehahn, has specialized in open-universe sandbox games for decades. Their X series allows players to explore hundreds of sectors, but even they must carefully tune travel times and station density to keep the experience engaging. The studio uses a mix of densely packed core systems and almost-empty frontier zones to give a sense of scale without boredom.

perspectives.description: Space games can ignite a lifelong passion for science, just as movies and books do. By making the cosmos feel vast yet playable, they give kids a way to ‘travel’ through star systems and spark curiosity about real physics and space exploration.

Wildly inaccurate scale risks giving players a false sense of how space works. If someone grows up thinking asteroid belts are dense rock fields, they may misunderstand the real challenges of spaceflight and the careful navigation needed for probes and spacecraft.

The tension between realism and fun is a classic design trade-off. No game can simulate the full, boring emptiness of deep space and still be entertaining; developers must pick a balance. The tricks they use reveal a lot about human perception and what feels believable.

Future games with virtual reality might allow for more patient, realistic space travel, where players can spend hours watching the stars drift. Advances in artificial intelligence could generate truly boundless universes, forcing developers to rethink how they teach distance and scale in interactive media.
